diagnostic_evidence.quote: Equation \eqref{eq:equation1} has a unique solution $x_*$ such that $\|a\|_{\w}+\|x_*\|_1<1$.
In this subsection, we show that equation \eqref{eq:equation1} admits a unique solution $x_*$.

issues.failure_explanation: The theorem proves uniqueness only within the class $\|x\|_1+\|a\|_{\mathcal W}<1$, but the abstract (and the opening sentence of Section 2.2) state uniqueness of a nonnegative solution without that restriction. The restriction is essential: take $n=1$, $a(z)=1/2$ (so $A=(2-1/2)-1/2=1$) and $b=1/10$, which satisfies $\|b\|_1<(1-\|a\|_{\mathcal W})^2=1/4$; the equation $x-x^2=0.1$ then has two nonnegative solutions $x=(1\pm\sqrt{0.6})/2\approx0.113$ and $\approx0.887$. Hence unqualified uniqueness of a nonnegative solution is false under the paper's own hypotheses.

failure_location.quote: Existence and uniqueness of a nonnegative solution is proved.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Qualify the abstract and the Section 2.2 sentence with 'such that $\|x\|_1+\|a\|_{\mathcal W}<1$'.
issues.overall_effect: The abstract and the Section 2.2 preamble overstate the scope of Theorem thm:solution, leading readers to expect global uniqueness of nonnegative solutions, which the equation does not possess.
issues.title: Abstract and Section 2.2 claim unqualified uniqueness of a nonnegative solution, which is false
issues.why_classification: A one-line qualification of the prose restores accuracy; the formal theorem and all proofs are correct within the stated class, so nothing of substance is lost.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: $b\in \mathbb R^n$ is a nonnegative vector such that $\|a\|_{\w}+\|b\|_1<1\quad {\rm and}\quad \|b\|_1<(1-\|a\|_{\w})^2$.

issues.failure_explanation: The hypotheses permit $b=0$, for which $g(0)=\|A^{-1}b\|_1=0$, so the claimed strict inequality in the proof of Theorem thm:solution is false; the same degenerate case makes the displayed strict inequality $\frac{2}{1-\|A^{-2}b\|_1}>2$ in the proof of Lemma lem:mu false (it equals 2). The conclusions still hold for $b=0$ ($x_*=0$ is the unique solution in the class, since $g$ is strictly decreasing with $g(\beta)=-\beta<0$), so only the sign argument needs repair.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Treat $b=0$ separately (then $x_*=0$ trivially) or replace the strict inequality by $g(0)\ge0$ and note that strict monotonicity still yields a unique root.
issues.overall_effect: The proof of Theorem thm:solution (and one step of the proof of Lemma lem:mu) is incomplete in the degenerate case $b=0$; the statements themselves remain true and all downstream uses are unaffected.
issues.title: Proof of thm:solution asserts g(0)>0, which is false for the allowed degenerate case b=0
issues.why_classification: A local degenerate-case check or a $>$ to $\ge$ fix preserves the statement, the method, and every downstream result; no substantive content is lost.

issues.failure_explanation: The proof cancels $\tau$ to conclude $\mu_*=\|(A-\mu_*I)^{-1}b\|_1$, which requires $\tau\ne0$; the lemma never assumes it. For $\tau=0$, $\mu_{k+1}=\mu_k$, so any constant $\mu_0=c\in[0,\beta]$ is a convergent sequence, but $x_k=(A-cI)^{-1}b$ is not a solution of the equation unless $c$ is the fixed point, contradicting the lemma's conclusion.

failure_location.quote: If the sequence $\{\mu_k\}$ converges to a constant $\mu_*\in [0,\beta]$, then the sequence $\{x_k\}$ generated by \eqref{para2},  converges to the unique solution $x_*$ of equation \eqref{eq:equation1}, and   $x_*=(A-\mu_* I)^{-1}b$.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Add the hypothesis $0<\tau$ (equivalently $\tau\ne0$) to the lemma's statement.
issues.overall_effect: The lemma is false as stated for $\tau=0$; its use in the convergence analysis of the relaxed iteration is unaffected because Lemma lem:mu assumes $0<\tau$.
issues.title: Lemma mu_and_x omits the hypothesis tau nonzero and is false for tau=0
issues.why_classification: Adding the missing hypothesis is a one-word local repair; every actual application of the lemma has $\tau>0$, so no result or guarantee is lost.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: We examine the effectiveness of the relaxed fixed-point iteration \eqref{para2}, Newton iteration \eqref{2.2} and the structure-preserving doubling algorithm \eqref{EPFQ2} in computing the solution $x_*$ of equation \eqref{eq:equation1} such that $\|x_*\|_1+\|M\|_{1}<1$.

issues.failure_explanation: The construction gives $\|b\|_1=(1-\|M\|_\infty-\sigma)^2$, while the claimed regime $\|x_*\|_1+\|M\|_1<1$ is only guaranteed when $\|b\|_1<(1-\|M\|_1)^2$, i.e. when $\|M\|_\infty+\sigma>\|M\|_1$; the construction neither enforces nor implies this. For instance, a random $M$ with $\|M\|_\infty$ slightly below $\|M\|_1$ (which for iid entries is as likely as the reverse) yields $\|b\|_1>(1-\|M\|_1)^2$, placing the instance outside the hypotheses of Theorem thm:solution and of the convergence analyses of all three algorithms.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Normalize $b$ with $(1-\|M\|_1-\sigma)^2$ instead of $(1-\|M\|_\infty-\sigma)^2$, which enforces the hypothesis directly.
issues.overall_effect: The numerical validation reported in Tables 2-3 may fall outside the regime where the paper's theorems guarantee existence and uniqueness of $x_*$ or the convergence of the relaxed fixed-point iteration, Newton iteration, and SDA.
issues.title: Example ex2 normalizes b with (1-||M||_infinity-sigma)^2, which need not satisfy the paper's hypothesis ||b||_1 < (1-||M||_1)^2
issues.why_classification: A one-line change to the experiment's construction restores the hypothesis; the algorithms and the theory are untouched, so there is no mathematical loss beyond re-running the experiments.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: Comparison of the  relaxed fixed-point iteration (RFPI), Newton iteration (NI) and SDA, when $n = 1000$, $\delta = 0.01$, $\sigma = 1\times 10^{-5}$.
Comparison of the  relaxed fixed-point iteration (RFPI), Newton iteration (NI) and SDA, when $n = 1000$, $\delta = 0.1$, $\sigma = 0.001$.

issues.failure_explanation: The prose sets the second experiment at $\delta=0.1$, $\sigma=0.001$ (matching the commented-out Table 3-1), but the printed Table 3 caption states $\delta=0.01$, $\sigma=1\times10^{-5}$; the two cannot both describe the same experiment, so the reported nearly-singular experiment is not reproducible as documented.

failure_location.quote: In this example, we set $n = 1000$, $\delta = 0.9$, $\sigma = 0.001$  and $n = 1000$, $\delta = 0.1$, $\sigma = 0.001 $, respectively.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Reconcile the caption with the prose (and the commented table) so that a single parameter set is documented.
issues.overall_effect: Ambiguity about the conditioning parameter $\delta$ in the 'nearly singular' experiment, weakening the reproducibility of the paper's efficiency comparison.
issues.title: Prose parameters for the second ex2 experiment contradict the printed Table 3 caption
issues.why_classification: Pure reporting inconsistency; correcting the caption or the sentence restores the documentation with no mathematical loss.

issues.failure_explanation: Per Table 2, Newton iteration uses 6 iterations and 0.5937s, versus 45 iterations and 1.0535s for RFPI and 6 iterations and 0.8514s for SDA; Newton is superior to RFPI in both iterations and time and is tied with SDA in iterations while faster in time. The sentence claiming Newton is inferior to both contradicts the paper's own data.

failure_location.quote: In the first case, Table \ref{table2} shows that  Newton iteration is inferior to both the SDA and the relaxed fixed-point iteration in terms of the number of iterations and CPU time.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Correct the sentence to state that Newton iteration is superior to (or at least not inferior to) SDA and RFPI in iterations and CPU time.
issues.overall_effect: The numerical conclusion drawn from Table 2 is backwards, misreporting which method is more efficient in the well-conditioned case.
issues.title: Commentary on Table 2 claims Newton iteration is inferior to SDA and RFPI, the opposite of the table
issues.why_classification: A one-sentence correction aligned with the table; no algorithm, theorem, or rate is affected.

issues.failure_explanation: For this example $\nu=\sqrt{\|v\|_1}=1$, and the paper's Theorem thm:lap forces $\|y\|_1=1$ (since $y=(W^{-1/2})^Tv$ and $W\mathbf{1}=\mathbf{1}$ imply $\mathbf{1}^Ty=\mathbf{1}^Tv=1$). The printed entries sum to $1.0300\ne1$, so the displayed vector cannot be the exact solution; consequently the reported comparison $\|x_N-y\|_1=8.7931e-12$ is measured against an erroneous reference vector.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Recompute and reprint $y$ so that it satisfies $\|y\|_1=1$ and the equation $(I+V^T)y-\|y\|_1y=v$.
issues.overall_effect: The reported 'exact' solution in Example L is inconsistent with the paper's own theorem, so the example's numerical validation of the improved Newton iteration rests on an incorrect reference vector.
issues.title: Printed 'exact' solution y in Example L has 1-norm 1.03, contradicting the proved identity ||y||_1 = nu = 1
issues.why_classification: Recomputing and correcting the displayed vector repairs the example; no theorem, algorithm, or rate is affected.
